questions.question: Q1
questions.text: Compare and contrast probability sampling and non-probability sampling.
questions.answer: Probability: every unit has a known, non-zero chance of selection (random); supports generalisation and sampling-error estimates. Non-probability: selection by convenience/judgement; cheaper and faster but risks bias and limits inference.

questions.question: Q1
questions.text: Compare and contrast stratified sampling and cluster sampling.
questions.answer: Stratified: split the population into homogeneous strata and sample within EVERY stratum (precision, representation of subgroups). Cluster: split into heterogeneous clusters that each mirror the population, randomly pick SOME clusters and survey them (cost/convenience, usually less precise).

questions.question: Q1
questions.topic: Quartiles, IQR and the 1.5×IQR outlier rule
questions.text: Show that if a data distribution has no outliers, the data points must be in the range [a, b] such that (Q3 − Q1) = (b − a)/4.
questions.answer: With the 1.5×IQR rule the fences are a = Q1 − 1.5·IQR and b = Q3 + 1.5·IQR, so b − a = (Q3 − Q1) + 3·IQR = 4·IQR, hence IQR = Q3 − Q1 = (b − a)/4.
questions.note: 10 marks for a two-line derivation: the lecturer rewards knowing the fence definitions.

questions.question: Q1
questions.text: Critically analyze the statement 'Correlation does not imply causation'.
questions.answer: Correlation measures linear association only; a third (confounding) variable, reverse causation or coincidence can produce it. Causation needs controlled experiments / mechanism.

questions.question: Q1
questions.text: Two scatter plots are given (both positive linear; one tight, one widely scattered). Analyze the relationships of both charts briefly.
questions.answer: Both show positive linear relationships; the first is strong (points close to the line, r near +1), the second weaker (more scatter, smaller r).

questions.question: Q2
questions.text: P(A) = 0.4, P(B) = 0.3 and P(A∪B) = 0.58. Are A and B independent?

questions.question: Q2
questions.text: P(A) = 0.8 and P(B) = 0.9 in a sample space S. Determine whether A and B are mutually exclusive.
questions.answer: If exclusive, P(A∪B) = 1.7 > 1, impossible. P(A∩B) ≥ 0.8 + 0.9 − 1 = 0.7 > 0, so NOT mutually exclusive.

questions.question: Q3
questions.topic: Type I vs Type II error
questions.text: Compare and contrast Type I error and Type II error in hypothesis testing.
questions.answer: Type I: reject a true H0 (probability α). Type II: fail to reject a false H0 (probability β). Lowering α (fixed n) raises β.

questions.question: Q3
questions.topic: CI for difference of means, pooled variance

questions.question: Q3
questions.topic: Hypotheses for a one-sided two-sample test
questions.text: 100 males (mean 78), 144 females (mean 74), common σ = 3. Write H0 and H1 to test whether males performed better.
questions.answer: H0: μM ≤ μF (or μM = μF); H1: μM > μF (right-tailed).

questions.question: Q3
questions.text: Test at 5% whether males performed better (z95% = 1.645).
questions.answer: z = (78 − 74) / (3√(1/100 + 1/144)) ≈ 10.24 > 1.645, reject H0: males performed better.

questions.question: Q4
questions.text: Mention two assumptions in linear regression and briefly explain.
questions.answer: Any two of: linearity; independence of errors; constant variance of errors (homoscedasticity); normally distributed errors; (multiple regression) no multicollinearity.

questions.question: Q4
questions.text: Gender (2 categories) and Extra_Curricular (3 categories) are categorical predictors of GPA. Explain how to convert them to dummy variables.
questions.answer: k categories give k − 1 dummies (0/1): Gender gives 1 dummy (e.g. Male = 1); Extra_Curricular gives 2 dummies (e.g. Societies, Sports) with 'No' as the baseline. Using k dummies causes the dummy-variable trap (perfect multicollinearity).

questions.text: Analyze the goodness of fit of the model using the R² from (c).
questions.answer: 86% of the variation in GPA is explained by the model; a good fit, but R² alone doesn't prove causation or validate the assumptions.

questions.question: Q4
questions.text: GPA-hat = 0.1 + 0.35 × Study_Hours. Interpret the intercept (0.1).

questions.question: Q4

questions.question: Q1
questions.text: A sample of size n has sample variance a. Treating that same sample as a population, its variance is b. Show n = a/(a − b).
questions.answer: a = S/(n − 1), b = S/n with S = Σ(x − x̄)², so a(n − 1) = bn, giving n(a − b) = a and n = a/(a − b).

questions.question: Q1
questions.given: figure: three histograms with mean/median/mode marked
questions.text: Critically discuss the behaviour of the mean, median and mode for three histograms (symmetric, right-skewed, left-skewed).
questions.answer: Symmetric: mean = median = mode. Right (positive) skew: mode < median < mean (the mean is pulled toward the tail). Left (negative) skew: mean < median < mode.

questions.question: Q1
questions.text: Target: mean energy-to-discovery ratio of 50 J per star over 5 days. Days 1–4: 3,800 J/70, 4,200/80, 3,500/60, 3,900/70. Day 5 generates 4,500 J. How many discoveries are needed on day 5?
questions.answer: Ratio of totals: (19,900)/(280 + x) = 50 gives x = 118. (Read as the mean of the daily ratios it gives about 154: the wording is ambiguous.)
questions.note: AMBIGUOUS wording in the original. A rule for mock writers: never write a question with two defensible readings.

questions.question: Q2

questions.text: Jenny was born between 26 and 30 August (exclusive); her birth year is unknown. Probability she was born on a Monday?
questions.answer: The birth year is unknown, so each candidate date's weekday is equally likely: P(Monday) = 1/7.

questions.question: Q2
questions.text: f(x) = Cx² for −1 < x < 2, 0 otherwise. Find C.
questions.answer: ∫ from −1 to 2 of Cx² dx = C(8/3 + 1/3) = 3C = 1, so C = 1/3.

questions.question: Q3
questions.text: Show that V(X) = E(X²) − (E(X))².
questions.answer: V(X) = E[(X − μ)²] = E(X²) − 2μE(X) + μ² = E(X²) − μ².

questions.question: Q3
questions.text: Briefly explain: a point estimator should be unbiased.
questions.answer: Its expected value equals the parameter: E(θ̂) = θ.

questions.question: Q3
questions.text: Briefly explain: a point estimator should be efficient.
questions.answer: Among unbiased estimators it has the smallest variance.

questions.question: Q3
questions.text: Explain the difference between a point estimator and an interval estimator.
questions.answer: A point estimator gives a single value (e.g. x̄); an interval estimator gives a range with a stated confidence level, which shows the uncertainty.

questions.question: Q01
questions.text: Why is proportionate stratified random sampling suitable for 4,000 students in 3 programs (CS 2,000; IT 1,200; DS 800)?
questions.answer: The programs differ in size and possibly in opinion; strata guarantee each is represented in proportion, which improves precision.

questions.question: Q01
questions.text: Allocate a sample of 200 proportionately.

questions.question: Q01
questions.text: Effect of selecting 100/50/50 instead?
questions.answer: IT is under-represented (50 vs 60) and DS over-represented (50 vs 40), so the sample is no longer proportional and estimates are biased unless weighted.

questions.question: Q02
questions.text: Times 18, 20, 21, 22, 24, 25, 80: mean, median, mode.
questions.answer: Mean 30, median 22, no mode.

questions.question: Q02
questions.text: Range and IQR (median-of-halves); outliers by the 1.5×IQR rule.
questions.answer: Range 62; Q1 20, Q3 25, IQR 5; fences 12.5 and 32.5, so 80 is an outlier.

questions.question: Q02

questions.answer: The mean is pulled up (30) and the median is resistant (22), so the median is more typical.

questions.question: Q03
questions.text: Difference between variance and standard deviation.
questions.answer: SD = √variance; SD is in the data's units, so it is easier to interpret.

questions.topic: Independent vs mutually exclusive; contingency tables
questions.text: Independent vs mutually exclusive, using 'uses app' and 'makes purchase'.
questions.answer: Mutually exclusive: they can't both occur (here they can: 180 did both). Independent: P(purchase | app) = P(purchase).

questions.question: Q05
questions.text: Prior vs conditional probability in baggage scanning.
questions.answer: Prior P(prohibited) = 0.04 before any scan; conditional P(prohibited | positive) after the evidence.

questions.question: Q05
questions.text: Base rate 4%, sensitivity 95%, false-positive rate 8%. P(prohibited | positive)?

questions.question: Q05
questions.text: Why a positive result doesn't necessarily mean a prohibited item.
questions.answer: The low base rate and the false positives on the 96% clean bags dominate the positives (base-rate effect).

questions.answer: Counts in a fixed interval, constant rate, independent events, mean = variance = λ.

questions.text: Importance of mean and SD for a normal distribution of delivery times.
questions.answer: The mean locates the centre; the SD sets the spread, and together they fix every probability.

questions.question: Q09
questions.text: Explain the memoryless property for network failures.
questions.answer: P(X > s + t | X > s) = P(X > t): past survival doesn't change future waiting.

questions.question: Q09

questions.answer: 1 − e^−0.3 ≈ 0.2592 (the same as from new).

questions.question: Q10
questions.text: Explain the CLT and why x̄ is approximately normal for a skewed population.
questions.answer: For large n the distribution of x̄ is approximately N(μ, σ²/n) whatever the population shape.

questions.question: Q10
questions.text: Effect of n going from 81 to 324.
questions.answer: SE halves (to 1): 4 times the sample size gives twice the precision.

questions.question: Q11
questions.text: Why the t-distribution for this CI?
questions.answer: σ is unknown and estimated by s, with a small sample from a normal population.

questions.question: Q11
questions.text: Does the CI support a 500 ml claim? Correct interpretation of a 95% CI.
questions.answer: 500 lies inside, so no evidence against the claim. 95% refers to the long-run proportion of such intervals that contain μ, not P(μ in this interval).

questions.question: Q12
questions.text: Hypotheses for the 20-hour battery claim (left-tailed); meaning of a Type I error.
questions.answer: H0: μ = 20 (≥ 20); H1: μ < 20. Type I = rejecting a true claim.

questions.answer: Additive: constant seasonal swings. Multiplicative: swings grow with the trend.
